task.goal: Design a quiet, repeatable activity for a train-station waiting area that lets travelers notice sounds without adding noise.
hard_constraints: One arts group has printed cards, a freestanding display permit and two weeks to prepare.
No recording, microphones, speakers, power, phone requirement or collection of personal information.
Do not block circulation; readable from a seated place, optional in under two minutes, and test against a plain poster.
task.available_resources: Station-approved display location and short volunteer observation periods.
task.expected_result: A specific silent interaction with accessibility and upkeep checks.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A silent listening score
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a large printed card on the freestanding display to guide a seated, one-minute sequence: “Stay seated. Notice one nearby sound. Notice one farther away. Notice a sound that comes and goes. Finish whenever you like.” Travelers participate entirely through attention; nothing needs touching, saying or submitting. The mechanism is a short sequence of contrasting listening tasks that gives ordinary station sounds a structure.

Success depends on the prompts being legible from the approved seats and on some audible variation being present. The sequence may become frustrating in a uniformly loud space, so add: “One sound is enough. There are no correct answers.” State that announcements take priority and discourage closing eyes or wearing headphones for the activity.

The arts group needs one main card, replacement copies and a two-week preparation schedule covering wording, a full-size print trial and station approval. Use large, high-contrast type, plain language, generous spacing and no information conveyed through color alone. Check actual seated sightlines before printing; shorten the text if necessary. Participation should require neither standing nor reaching. A small line acknowledges that listening may be inaccessible or uncomfortable and that passing is welcome.

Keep the display wholly within its permitted footprint. Volunteers check stability, glare, damaged cards and visibility after seating or station conditions change. The activity is repeatable because the same score encounters different sounds; no daily content changes are necessary.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate the score with a plain poster saying “Take a moment to notice the sounds around you,” using the same position and comparable typography during several short, similar waiting periods. Volunteers tally only aggregate looks and obvious circulation problems; gaze alone does not establish listening. With station approval, invite a few seated travelers to answer voluntarily by pointing to printed options: noticed a sound, unclear, or preferred not to participate. Keep anonymous totals only. Revise or reject the score if it is unreadable from the seats, creates pressure to finish, draws people into the walkway, or shows no clearer usefulness than the plain poster.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Find the return
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Place one large printed challenge on the display: “Choose a sound already happening. Listen for whether it returns. Stop after its next return—or after about a minute.” Beneath it, show three equally valid endings: “It returned,” “It changed,” and “Something else caught my attention.” Travelers select an ending mentally; there are no movable parts or public responses.

The primary mechanism is anticipation: choosing one sound and waiting for its recurrence can make small variations noticeable. Unlike a sequence of attention prompts, this activity follows a traveler’s own selected sound over time. It can be repeated with another sound on another visit.

It assumes at least one distinguishable sound is available. Irregular or continuous station noise may make recurrence unclear; explicitly accept “I couldn’t tell” and avoid suggesting that anyone wait for a particular train, announcement or operational signal. Include “Announcements come first. Stay seated and keep your eyes available.” No counting accuracy or timing device is needed, and the activity ends whenever the traveler chooses.

Preparation requires a single full-size card, spare prints and seated readability checks within the two weeks. Use high contrast, large type and simple wording. Explain “returns” as “happens again” to reduce language demands. Acknowledge that travelers who cannot or do not wish to listen can skip the activity without missing any station information. Do not frame this as a hearing test.

Mount the card within the approved freestanding footprint, facing the seats rather than passing traffic. Volunteers check that all text remains visible, the stand is stable and the invitation does not cause people to approach. Upkeep consists of replacing worn cards and checking that nearby operational notices remain unobstructed.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare brief, matched display periods against a plain listening poster in the same location. In a small optional seated user check, ask participants to point to whether they understood what to do and whether following a returning sound helped them notice something. Record aggregate answers only, without describing their chosen sounds or collecting personal information. Reject or simplify the challenge if several users interpret it as requiring a scheduled event, continue beyond two minutes, cannot identify an acceptable ending, or find it less useful than the plain invitation.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Sound and its description
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Display a short, large-print word palette: “steady / uneven,” “sharp / soft,” and “near / far.” The invitation reads: “Notice one sound. Silently choose a word that fits it—or imagine your own. Listen once more: does the word still fit? Finish whenever you like.” Nothing is marked or collected. The mechanism is description followed by reconsideration: trying a word can direct attention toward a sound’s qualities and reveal that the first description was incomplete.

This is independently usable as a single printed card. It does not ask travelers to locate sound sources, identify people, move around or distinguish a correct answer. Include “A sound can fit both words, neither word, or change.” That prevents the pairs from becoming a classification test. The experience should take roughly 30–90 seconds, with an explicit invitation to stop immediately for announcements or departure.

The main assumptions are that the traveler can access some sound and understand the small vocabulary. Language and hearing differences limit reach; use familiar words, explain the task in one sentence and make skipping explicitly acceptable. Avoid pictures that imply every sound has an obvious visible source. Large, high-contrast text must be readable from the actual approved seats, with no reliance on color, fine print or touching the stand.

Within two weeks, the group can draft the card, conduct a full-size seated trial, obtain station approval and print replacements. The display stays entirely inside its permitted location and does not invite people to gather. Volunteers inspect glare, legibility, stability and obstruction during short visits. Because travelers supply their own sound and interpretation, the card needs no regular content refresh.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate this card with a plain poster inviting travelers to notice surrounding sounds, keeping placement and visual prominence similar. Offer a few willing seated travelers an anonymous, optional pointing check: easy to understand, confusing, or felt like a test; also ask whether reconsidering a word helped them notice a quality. Retain only aggregate counts. The mechanism is weakened if users merely read the words without listening again. Revise or reject it if the vocabulary repeatedly confuses people, suggests correct answers, requires approaching the display, or offers no perceived benefit over the plain poster.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Predict, then listen
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The display reads: “Stay seated. Choose a visible, non-person feature: a clock, door or sign. Silently guess: will it make a sound? Listen briefly. Did what you heard fit your guess? ‘I couldn’t tell’ is a complete ending. Stop whenever you like—about half a minute is enough. Announcements come first.” No answer is submitted and no movement is requested.

The mechanism is prediction followed by comparison. A traveler’s visual expectation gives listening a specific question; an unexpected sound or an apparently silent object can expose a difference between what the scene suggests and what is audible. Unlike describing an existing sound, the activity begins with a visual prediction. Repeat visits can use different features.

It assumes that an appropriate stationary feature is visible from the approved seats. Sound sources can be ambiguous, so the card must say that hearing something does not establish which object caused it. Avoid examples involving people, safety equipment or waiting for a train. The activity may be unsuitable where looking toward a feature distracts from essential information.

Within two weeks, the arts group can inspect seated views, draft and approve one large card, trial a full-size print and prepare replacements. Use plain language, high contrast and lettering verified from the intended seats. No touching, standing, accurate timing or hearing acuity test is involved. Include a prominent invitation to pass if looking or listening is inaccessible or uncomfortable. Volunteers check stand stability, glare, damage and circulation; replace the card if changing surroundings remove suitable visible features.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate the activity with a plain “Notice the sounds around you” poster at the same location during comparable short periods. Ask a few consenting seated travelers, without retaining personal information, whether they could choose a feature, understood that its sound source might remain uncertain, and noticed anything through checking their prediction. Keep aggregate totals only. Reject or revise if people approach objects, confuse guesses with source identification, exceed two minutes, or report no useful difference from the plain poster. Observation alone cannot establish whether the prediction mechanism worked.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Give a sound a silent partner
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The card invites: “Listen briefly to the station. Imagine one quiet line of a film subtitle for what you hear. Keep it in your head. Listen again: would you keep that line or change it? One line is enough; stop whenever you like.” Offer one clearly imaginary example: “[A little bustle before departure.]” Add “Announcements come first. Stay seated; there is nothing to write or share.”

The mechanism is imaginative scene-making. Turning the whole audible setting into an imagined subtitle can make travelers consider how several sounds contribute to a scene, rather than tracking one sound or assigning it a descriptive word. Listening again gives the imagined line a chance to change. Travelers can repeat the activity as the station’s soundscape changes.

This assumes some access to sound and comfort with imagining language. It may appeal unevenly across languages, literacy levels and preferences; there is no evidence here that a creative framing improves attention. Avoid asking travelers to invent dialogue, interpret strangers’ emotions or transcribe conversations. The card should explicitly allow a single imagined word or passing entirely, and explain that this is play, with no correct answer.

Implementation needs one approved large-print card, replacements and a full-size seated trial within the two weeks. Keep the invitation short enough to read without approaching, use high contrast and generous spacing, and distinguish it visually from operational information. The stand remains within its permitted footprint. Volunteers check readability, stability, wear and any gathering in the walkway. No materials are distributed, so upkeep requires only inspection and replacement.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare matched periods displaying this card and a plain listening poster. In a brief optional seated check, ask whether the instruction was understandable, whether imagining a subtitle prompted another listen, and whether inventing wording distracted from actual sounds. Retain only anonymous aggregate answers; do not request the invented lines. Reject or simplify if users mainly compose stories without listening, feel pressured to be creative, need explanations that defeat independent use, or find no benefit over the plain poster. Also reject any layout that requires approaching the stand or delays attention to announcements.

DIRECT_FULL.title: What stayed in memory?
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The display offers a brief listening-and-memory loop: “Stay seated. Listen to the station for a few moments. Silently recall one sound from those moments. Listen again: is anything audible that your memory left out? One discovery—or no difference—is enough. Finish whenever you like; about a minute is plenty. Announcements come first.” Nothing is spoken, touched, written or submitted.

The mechanism is comparison between a remembered soundscape and current perception. Memory preserves only part of a busy scene; checking what was omitted may bring an overlooked sound into attention. Unlike predicting an object's sound or revisiting a descriptive word, the traveler uses their own recent memory as the comparison. The same instructions remain usable on subsequent visits.

This assumes some access to sound and willingness to recall a brief experience. It may impose unwanted memory demands, and changing station sounds can make comparison ambiguous. Include: “This is not a memory test. Sounds may have changed. No need to identify what made them.” Passing is explicitly welcome, including when listening is inaccessible or uncomfortable. Do not ask travelers to close their eyes or reproduce sounds.

Within two weeks, the group can draft and obtain approval for one printed display card, trial a full-size copy from the intended seats, and print replacements. Use large, high-contrast lettering, short lines and no color-dependent instructions. Keep essential wording readable without approaching. Mount everything within the permitted footprint, clearly distinguished from station information. During short observation visits, volunteers check stability, glare, wear, seated sightlines and any attraction into the walkway. No consumables or content rotation are needed.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate the activity and a plain “Notice the sounds around you” poster during comparable short periods in the same position. With station approval, conduct a few optional seated checks using printed response choices and silent pointing. Ask whether recall prompted another listen, felt confusing, or felt like a memory test; ask whether the second listen revealed something previously unnoticed. Retain aggregate totals only, with no personal information. Observed looking cannot establish participation. Simplify or reject the activity if users need explanation, feel tested, approach the stand, take over two minutes, or report no additional usefulness over the plain poster. Reports of new sounds support usefulness but cannot establish that those sounds were previously present and overlooked.

EXPAND.title: Look, predict, listen
EXPAND.proposal:
A printed card invites travelers to compare visual expectation with actual hearing: “Stay seated. Look at one ordinary thing you can already see. Guess silently: will you hear it? Listen briefly. Did you hear it, hear something else, or remain unsure? Finish here.” The mechanism is a prediction followed by a sensory check. A visible object may suggest a sound that is absent or masked, while listening may reveal something outside the traveler’s initial visual attention. No source identification needs to be correct.

The activity takes roughly 20–60 seconds, requires no response and can be repeated with another visible object. Ask travelers to choose an object rather than a person, and never to move for a better view. Include “Do not make a sound to check. Announcements and your journey come first. Stop whenever you wish.”

It assumes access to both the visual scene and some sound. It will not suit everyone with limited vision or hearing; explicitly welcome skipping and do not present the exercise as a sensory test. Use plain language, large high-contrast print and no color-dependent instructions. All essential text must be readable from the approved seats, without reaching or approaching.

Within two weeks, the arts group can draft one display card, test a full-size paper version from the seats, secure wording approval and print replacements. The stand remains within its permitted footprint. Short volunteer visits check stability, glare, worn print, seated sightlines and whether viewers gather near it. The content needs no scheduled refresh because the visible scene supplies new starting points.
EXPAND.experiment: Alternate the card with a similarly prominent plain poster saying “Take a moment to notice the sounds around you” during comparable short periods. In a few optional seated checks, travelers can silently point to printed answers indicating whether they made a prediction and whether listening surprised them, confirmed it or remained unclear. Keep anonymous aggregate totals only. Inspect whether anyone approaches an object or deliberately makes noise. Simplify or reject the interaction if it encourages either behavior, exceeds two minutes in observed user checks, or users report no added noticing beyond the plain poster. Looking at the display alone is not evidence of participation.

EXPAND.title: Imagine one sound missing
EXPAND.proposal:
The display offers a short counterfactual exercise: “Notice the sounds around you. Choose one you can hear. Imagine this place without that sound for a moment. Listen again: what else is still there? Finish whenever you like.” Travelers make no marks and do not need to report which sound they chose.

The mechanism is imagined subtraction. Mentally removing a prominent element may make the remaining soundscape easier to attend to. The outcome changes through a comparison between the actual scene and an imagined absence, rather than through describing a sound or waiting for it to return. The card must clarify: “You do not have to stop hearing the sound. Just imagine.” This is an invitation, not a claim that imagination can remove acoustic masking.

Allow about 30–60 seconds. Include “Keep your eyes available. Announcements come first. Skipping or stopping is welcome.” Avoid language about eliminating annoying sounds, which could turn the exercise into an unwanted focus on discomfort. It assumes that a traveler can hear something and finds this small imaginative task understandable; some people will find it difficult or unhelpful.

Preparation needs one main printed card, spare copies and a full-size seated wording trial, all feasible within two weeks. Use large, high-contrast text with the action in a few short lines. Hearing and language access remain limitations; disclose that listening is optional without implying that participation assesses ability. Position the approved stand toward the seats, entirely inside its footprint, with no materials to collect. Volunteers check glare, stability, print condition, operational-notice visibility and any tendency for people to approach.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare short, matched periods showing this card and a plain listening poster in the same location. A few willing seated travelers can point to “imagined it missing,” “instruction unclear” or “preferred to stop,” followed by whether another sound became noticeable. Retain only aggregate counts. The smallest useful critique is whether readers understand imagination as the task rather than attempting to block their ears or move away. Reject or rewrite the card if that misunderstanding recurs, if the exercise increases reported discomfort, or if the extra instruction offers no perceived benefit over the plain poster. This check cannot establish that imagined subtraction improves hearing.

EXPAND.title: Hear the overlap
EXPAND.proposal:
A large printed card asks: “Can you notice two sounds happening together? Listen to them as one little scene for a few breaths. One sound, a blur, or uncertainty is also a complete ending.” Nothing is selected publicly, touched or submitted. The traveler can finish immediately and should normally need less than a minute.

The mechanism is perceptual grouping: attention shifts toward the relationship between simultaneous sounds. Two otherwise separate events may briefly form a combined texture or accidental accompaniment. Unlike choosing descriptive words or following a returning sound, the invitation depends on hearing coexistence. It does not ask travelers to count precisely, identify sources, find a rhythm or wait for a particular combination.

This assumes that at least two sounds are distinguishable at some point. In a strongly masked or uniform environment, the intended experience may not occur; the printed acceptance of one sound or uncertainty prevents an open-ended search. Include “Do not make sounds to join in. Stay seated. Announcements and departures take priority.” Avoid musical notation or an instruction to tap, which could encourage audible participation.

The group needs a single main card, replacements and a full-size readability trial within the two-week preparation window. Use familiar language, generous spacing, high contrast and text sized for the actual approved seats. Participation requires neither a device nor physical interaction. Acknowledge that listening may be inaccessible or uncomfortable and that passing is welcome.

The approved stand faces the seating and stays within its footprint. Short volunteer inspections cover stability, glare, damage, obstruction of station information and any gathering in circulation space. No changing daily content is necessary: different overlapping sounds supply variation.
EXPAND.experiment: Alternate this card with a plain poster inviting travelers to notice surrounding sounds, using comparable placement and typography. Offer a small optional seated pointing check: “noticed sounds together,” “heard one or could not tell,” or “unclear what to do.” Ask separately whether the prompt helped them notice anything beyond the general invitation; retain anonymous totals only. Observe for tapping, vocal imitation, standing to search or prolonged waiting. Reject or simplify the prompt if it induces those behaviors, repeatedly requires explanation, or provides no reported advantage over the plain poster. Silent observation alone cannot show whether perceptual grouping occurred.

EXPAND.title: What stayed in memory?
EXPAND.proposal:
Use the display to invite a brief comparison between hearing and remembering: “Stay seated. Listen to the sounds around you for a few moments. Now silently remember what you just heard. Listen again. Did anything escape your memory? Finding nothing new is a complete ending.” Add: “Finish within about a minute, or whenever you wish. Keep your eyes open. Announcements and your journey come first. Please make no sounds.” Nothing is touched, submitted or taken away.

The mechanism is a memory comparison: a short remembered impression becomes a reference against which travelers hear the present scene. Something omitted from memory may become noticeable on the second listen. Unlike tracking a returning sound, the exercise concerns what attention retained from the whole scene. Repeating it on another visit produces a different reference.

It assumes access to some sound and comfort with a small memory task. Memory differences, changing station sounds and acoustic masking mean that a newly noticed sound cannot reliably be attributed to forgetting. Present this as curiosity, never a memory or hearing test. Explicitly welcome skipping; the activity does not provide an equivalent experience for everyone with hearing or reading access needs.

Within two weeks, the group can prepare one large, high-contrast printed card, check the wording and actual seated sightlines, obtain station approval and print spares. All instructions must fit at a size readable from the approved seats. The freestanding display stays inside its permitted footprint. Short volunteer visits check stability, glare, damaged print, visibility of operational information and any tendency to approach or obstruct circulation.
EXPAND.experiment: Before final printing, have a few arts-group members independently try the card from the approved seats and a plain poster reading “Notice the sounds around you,” alternating which comes first. After each silent trial, privately consider whether another sound became noticeable and whether the instructions were clear; retain no participant information or recordings. Discuss impressions elsewhere. Reject or simplify the memory step if it feels like a test, regularly exceeds two minutes, or provides no useful difference from the poster. This is a small usability critique, not evidence of effectiveness for travelers generally.

Announcements come first.” No answer is submitted and no movement is requested.

The mechanism is prediction followed by comparison. A traveler’s visual expectation gives listening a specific question; an unexpected sound or an apparently silent object can expose a difference between what the scene suggests and what is audible. Unlike describing an existing sound, the activity begins with a visual prediction. Repeat visits can use different features.

It assumes that an appropriate stationary feature is visible from the approved seats. Sound sources can be ambiguous, so the card must say that hearing something does not establish which object caused it. Avoid examples involving people, safety equipment or waiting for a train. The activity may be unsuitable where looking toward a feature distracts from essential information.

Within two weeks, the arts group can inspect seated views, draft and approve one large card, trial a full-size print and prepare replacements. Use plain language, high contrast and lettering verified from the intended seats. No touching, standing, accurate timing or hearing acuity test is involved. Include a prominent invitation to pass if looking or listening is inaccessible or uncomfortable. Volunteers check stand stability, glare, damage and circulation; replace the card if changing surroundings remove suitable visible features.
REFINE.experiment: Alternate the activity with a plain “Notice the sounds around you” poster at the same location during comparable short periods. Ask a few consenting seated travelers, without retaining personal information, whether they could choose a feature, understood that its sound source might remain uncertain, and noticed anything through checking their prediction. Keep aggregate totals only. Reject or revise if people approach objects, confuse guesses with source identification, exceed two minutes, or report no useful difference from the plain poster. Observation alone cannot establish whether the prediction mechanism worked.

REFINE.title: Give a sound a silent partner
REFINE.proposal:
The card invites: “Listen briefly to the station. Imagine one quiet line of a film subtitle for what you hear. Keep it in your head. Listen again: would you keep that line or change it? One line is enough; stop whenever you like.” Offer one clearly imaginary example: “[A little bustle before departure.]” Add “Announcements come first. Stay seated; there is nothing to write or share.”

The mechanism is imaginative scene-making. Turning the whole audible setting into an imagined subtitle can make travelers consider how several sounds contribute to a scene, rather than tracking one sound or assigning it a descriptive word. Listening again gives the imagined line a chance to change. Travelers can repeat the activity as the station’s soundscape changes.

This assumes some access to sound and comfort with imagining language. It may appeal unevenly across languages, literacy levels and preferences; there is no evidence here that a creative framing improves attention. Avoid asking travelers to invent dialogue, interpret strangers’ emotions or transcribe conversations. The card should explicitly allow a single imagined word or passing entirely, and explain that this is play, with no correct answer.

Implementation needs one approved large-print card, replacements and a full-size seated trial within the two weeks. Keep the invitation short enough to read without approaching, use high contrast and generous spacing, and distinguish it visually from operational information. The stand remains within its permitted footprint. Volunteers check readability, stability, wear and any gathering in the walkway. No materials are distributed, so upkeep requires only inspection and replacement.
REFINE.experiment: Compare matched periods displaying this card and a plain listening poster. In a brief optional seated check, ask whether the instruction was understandable, whether imagining a subtitle prompted another listen, and whether inventing wording distracted from actual sounds. Retain only anonymous aggregate answers; do not request the invented lines. Reject or simplify if users mainly compose stories without listening, feel pressured to be creative, need explanations that defeat independent use, or find no benefit over the plain poster. Also reject any layout that requires approaching the stand or delays attention to announcements.

REFINE.title: A silent listening score without distance guessing
REFINE.proposal:
Repair of candidate 0. The specific weakness is that “nearby” and “farther away” ask travelers to infer sound-source distance, which station echoes and overlapping noise can make unreliable. That can turn a simple attention exercise into a source-location puzzle. Replace only those two prompts with attention-based contrasts, preserving the short listening sequence.

Print this seated-facing score: “Stay seated. Notice the sound that stands out most. Notice another sound, if one is easy to hear. Notice whether either sound continues, changes or stops. One brief listen is enough—finish within a minute, or stop whenever you like. Nothing to say, touch or submit. Announcements come first.” Add a clearly readable line: “One sound is enough. If listening is inaccessible or uncomfortable, passing is welcome.”

The changed action is to shift attention between audible sounds without judging their distance. This matters because the activity can work even when travelers cannot identify sources or hear beyond the dominant noise. It remains repeatable as the surrounding sounds change.

Prerequisites are station approval of the wording, a stable stand wholly inside the permitted footprint, and a full-size print readable from the intended seats. Within two weeks, draft, trial, approve and print the card and replacements. Use large, high-contrast type, generous spacing and no color-dependent instructions. Short volunteer visits check glare, wear, stability, seated visibility and circulation. No equipment, power, phones or personal information are needed. The remaining limit is that dominant noise may mask every other sound; the one-sound ending supports completion but cannot create audible variety.
REFINE.experiment: First show the full-size card to a few willing seated travelers using a silent printed invitation. Afterward, offer optional pointing choices: “noticed sounds,” “searched for where sounds came from,” or “unclear.” Keep aggregate totals only. Repeated source-searching or needing to approach the card falsifies the repair’s immediate usability. Then alternate the score and a plain “Notice the sounds around you” poster in the same position during comparable short periods, reversing their order. Use the same optional pointing question about whether the display helped participants notice a sound, plus aggregate circulation observations. If the score adds confusion or offers no reported benefit over the plain poster, simplify or retain the plain poster; looking at either display alone is not evidence of listening.

SAVE.title: A silent listening score
SAVE.proposal:
Use a large printed card on the freestanding display to guide a seated, one-minute sequence: “Stay seated. Notice one nearby sound. Notice one farther away. Notice a sound that comes and goes. Finish whenever you like.” Travelers participate entirely through attention; nothing needs touching, saying or submitting. The mechanism is a short sequence of contrasting listening tasks that gives ordinary station sounds a structure.

Success depends on the prompts being legible from the approved seats and on some audible variation being present. The sequence may become frustrating in a uniformly loud space, so add: “One sound is enough. There are no correct answers.” State that announcements take priority and discourage closing eyes or wearing headphones for the activity.

The arts group needs one main card, replacement copies and a two-week preparation schedule covering wording, a full-size print trial and station approval. Use large, high-contrast type, plain language, generous spacing and no information conveyed through color alone. Check actual seated sightlines before printing; shorten the text if necessary. Participation should require neither standing nor reaching. A small line acknowledges that listening may be inaccessible or uncomfortable and that passing is welcome.

Keep the display wholly within its permitted footprint. Volunteers check stability, glare, damaged cards and visibility after seating or station conditions change. The activity is repeatable because the same score encounters different sounds; no daily content changes are necessary.
SAVE.experiment: Alternate the score with a plain poster saying “Take a moment to notice the sounds around you,” using the same position and comparable typography during several short, similar waiting periods. Volunteers tally only aggregate looks and obvious circulation problems; gaze alone does not establish listening. With station approval, invite a few seated travelers to answer voluntarily by pointing to printed options: noticed a sound, unclear, or preferred not to participate. Keep anonymous totals only. Revise or reject the score if it is unreadable from the seats, creates pressure to finish, draws people into the walkway, or shows no clearer usefulness than the plain poster.

SAVE.title: Find the return
SAVE.proposal:
Place one large printed challenge on the display: “Choose a sound already happening. Listen for whether it returns. Stop after its next return—or after about a minute.” Beneath it, show three equally valid endings: “It returned,” “It changed,” and “Something else caught my attention.” Travelers select an ending mentally; there are no movable parts or public responses.

The primary mechanism is anticipation: choosing one sound and waiting for its recurrence can make small variations noticeable. Unlike a sequence of attention prompts, this activity follows a traveler’s own selected sound over time. It can be repeated with another sound on another visit.

It assumes at least one distinguishable sound is available. Irregular or continuous station noise may make recurrence unclear; explicitly accept “I couldn’t tell” and avoid suggesting that anyone wait for a particular train, announcement or operational signal. Include “Announcements come first. Stay seated and keep your eyes available.” No counting accuracy or timing device is needed, and the activity ends whenever the traveler chooses.

Preparation requires a single full-size card, spare prints and seated readability checks within the two weeks. Use high contrast, large type and simple wording. Explain “returns” as “happens again” to reduce language demands. Acknowledge that travelers who cannot or do not wish to listen can skip the activity without missing any station information. Do not frame this as a hearing test.

Mount the card within the approved freestanding footprint, facing the seats rather than passing traffic. Volunteers check that all text remains visible, the stand is stable and the invitation does not cause people to approach. Upkeep consists of replacing worn cards and checking that nearby operational notices remain unobstructed.
SAVE.experiment: Compare brief, matched display periods against a plain listening poster in the same location. In a small optional seated user check, ask participants to point to whether they understood what to do and whether following a returning sound helped them notice something. Record aggregate answers only, without describing their chosen sounds or collecting personal information. Reject or simplify the challenge if several users interpret it as requiring a scheduled event, continue beyond two minutes, cannot identify an acceptable ending, or find it less useful than the plain invitation.

SAVE.title: Sound and its description
SAVE.proposal:
Display a short, large-print word palette: “steady / uneven,” “sharp / soft,” and “near / far.” The invitation reads: “Notice one sound. Silently choose a word that fits it—or imagine your own. Listen once more: does the word still fit? Finish whenever you like.” Nothing is marked or collected. The mechanism is description followed by reconsideration: trying a word can direct attention toward a sound’s qualities and reveal that the first description was incomplete.

This is independently usable as a single printed card. It does not ask travelers to locate sound sources, identify people, move around or distinguish a correct answer. Include “A sound can fit both words, neither word, or change.” That prevents the pairs from becoming a classification test. The experience should take roughly 30–90 seconds, with an explicit invitation to stop immediately for announcements or departure.

The main assumptions are that the traveler can access some sound and understand the small vocabulary. Language and hearing differences limit reach; use familiar words, explain the task in one sentence and make skipping explicitly acceptable. Avoid pictures that imply every sound has an obvious visible source. Large, high-contrast text must be readable from the actual approved seats, with no reliance on color, fine print or touching the stand.

Within two weeks, the group can draft the card, conduct a full-size seated trial, obtain station approval and print replacements. The display stays entirely inside its permitted location and does not invite people to gather. Volunteers inspect glare, legibility, stability and obstruction during short visits. Because travelers supply their own sound and interpretation, the card needs no regular content refresh.
SAVE.experiment: Alternate this card with a plain poster inviting travelers to notice surrounding sounds, keeping placement and visual prominence similar. Offer a few willing seated travelers an anonymous, optional pointing check: easy to understand, confusing, or felt like a test; also ask whether reconsidering a word helped them notice a quality. Retain only aggregate counts. The mechanism is weakened if users merely read the words without listening again. Revise or reject it if the vocabulary repeatedly confuses people, suggests correct answers, requires approaching the display, or offers no perceived benefit over the plain poster.

SAVE.title: Look, predict, listen
SAVE.proposal:
A printed card invites travelers to compare visual expectation with actual hearing: “Stay seated. Look at one ordinary thing you can already see. Guess silently: will you hear it? Listen briefly. Did you hear it, hear something else, or remain unsure? Finish here.” The mechanism is a prediction followed by a sensory check. A visible object may suggest a sound that is absent or masked, while listening may reveal something outside the traveler’s initial visual attention. No source identification needs to be correct.

The activity takes roughly 20–60 seconds, requires no response and can be repeated with another visible object. Ask travelers to choose an object rather than a person, and never to move for a better view. Include “Do not make a sound to check. Announcements and your journey come first. Stop whenever you wish.”

It assumes access to both the visual scene and some sound. It will not suit everyone with limited vision or hearing; explicitly welcome skipping and do not present the exercise as a sensory test. Use plain language, large high-contrast print and no color-dependent instructions. All essential text must be readable from the approved seats, without reaching or approaching.

Within two weeks, the arts group can draft one display card, test a full-size paper version from the seats, secure wording approval and print replacements. The stand remains within its permitted footprint. Short volunteer visits check stability, glare, worn print, seated sightlines and whether viewers gather near it. The content needs no scheduled refresh because the visible scene supplies new starting points.
SAVE.experiment: Alternate the card with a similarly prominent plain poster saying “Take a moment to notice the sounds around you” during comparable short periods. In a few optional seated checks, travelers can silently point to printed answers indicating whether they made a prediction and whether listening surprised them, confirmed it or remained unclear. Keep anonymous aggregate totals only. Inspect whether anyone approaches an object or deliberately makes noise. Simplify or reject the interaction if it encourages either behavior, exceeds two minutes in observed user checks, or users report no added noticing beyond the plain poster. Looking at the display alone is not evidence of participation.

SAVE.title: Imagine one sound missing
SAVE.proposal:
The display offers a short counterfactual exercise: “Notice the sounds around you. Choose one you can hear. Imagine this place without that sound for a moment. Listen again: what else is still there? Finish whenever you like.” Travelers make no marks and do not need to report which sound they chose.

The mechanism is imagined subtraction. Mentally removing a prominent element may make the remaining soundscape easier to attend to. The outcome changes through a comparison between the actual scene and an imagined absence, rather than through describing a sound or waiting for it to return. The card must clarify: “You do not have to stop hearing the sound. Just imagine.” This is an invitation, not a claim that imagination can remove acoustic masking.

Allow about 30–60 seconds. Include “Keep your eyes available. Announcements come first. Skipping or stopping is welcome.” Avoid language about eliminating annoying sounds, which could turn the exercise into an unwanted focus on discomfort. It assumes that a traveler can hear something and finds this small imaginative task understandable; some people will find it difficult or unhelpful.

Preparation needs one main printed card, spare copies and a full-size seated wording trial, all feasible within two weeks. Use large, high-contrast text with the action in a few short lines. Hearing and language access remain limitations; disclose that listening is optional without implying that participation assesses ability. Position the approved stand toward the seats, entirely inside its footprint, with no materials to collect. Volunteers check glare, stability, print condition, operational-notice visibility and any tendency for people to approach.
SAVE.experiment: Compare short, matched periods showing this card and a plain listening poster in the same location. A few willing seated travelers can point to “imagined it missing,” “instruction unclear” or “preferred to stop,” followed by whether another sound became noticeable. Retain only aggregate counts. The smallest useful critique is whether readers understand imagination as the task rather than attempting to block their ears or move away. Reject or rewrite the card if that misunderstanding recurs, if the exercise increases reported discomfort, or if the extra instruction offers no perceived benefit over the plain poster. This check cannot establish that imagined subtraction improves hearing.

SAVE.title: Hear the overlap
SAVE.proposal:
A large printed card asks: “Can you notice two sounds happening together? Listen to them as one little scene for a few breaths. One sound, a blur, or uncertainty is also a complete ending.” Nothing is selected publicly, touched or submitted. The traveler can finish immediately and should normally need less than a minute.

The mechanism is perceptual grouping: attention shifts toward the relationship between simultaneous sounds. Two otherwise separate events may briefly form a combined texture or accidental accompaniment. Unlike choosing descriptive words or following a returning sound, the invitation depends on hearing coexistence. It does not ask travelers to count precisely, identify sources, find a rhythm or wait for a particular combination.

This assumes that at least two sounds are distinguishable at some point. In a strongly masked or uniform environment, the intended experience may not occur; the printed acceptance of one sound or uncertainty prevents an open-ended search. Include “Do not make sounds to join in. Stay seated. Announcements and departures take priority.” Avoid musical notation or an instruction to tap, which could encourage audible participation.

The group needs a single main card, replacements and a full-size readability trial within the two-week preparation window. Use familiar language, generous spacing, high contrast and text sized for the actual approved seats. Participation requires neither a device nor physical interaction. Acknowledge that listening may be inaccessible or uncomfortable and that passing is welcome.

The approved stand faces the seating and stays within its footprint. Short volunteer inspections cover stability, glare, damage, obstruction of station information and any gathering in circulation space. No changing daily content is necessary: different overlapping sounds supply variation.
SAVE.experiment: Alternate this card with a plain poster inviting travelers to notice surrounding sounds, using comparable placement and typography. Offer a small optional seated pointing check: “noticed sounds together,” “heard one or could not tell,” or “unclear what to do.” Ask separately whether the prompt helped them notice anything beyond the general invitation; retain anonymous totals only. Observe for tapping, vocal imitation, standing to search or prolonged waiting. Reject or simplify the prompt if it induces those behaviors, repeatedly requires explanation, or provides no reported advantage over the plain poster. Silent observation alone cannot show whether perceptual grouping occurred.
